subject: history
title: British Colonial Rule in Bengal
summary: This chapter covers the establishment and impact of British colonial rule in Bengal, from the Battle of Plassey through the East India Company's exploitation, the Bengal Famine, and the rise of Bengali nationalism that eventually led to the partition of Bengal and the independence movement.

sections.title: The Battle of Plassey and Battle of Buxar
sections.content: The Battle of Plassey was fought on June 23, 1757, between the British East India Company led by Robert Clive and the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj-ud-Daulah. Siraj-ud-Daulah was defeated due to the betrayal of Mir Jafar, his commander-in-chief, who had secretly allied with the British. This battle marked the beginning of British political influence in Bengal and India. The Battle of Buxar in 1764 was fought between the British and the combined forces of Mir Qasim (the Nawab of Bengal), Shuja-ud-Daulah (the Nawab of Awadh), and Shah Alam II (the Mughal Emperor). The British victory at Buxar established them as the dominant power in Bengal and granted them the diwani (right to collect revenue) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa in 1765.

sections.title: East India Company Rule and Exploitation
sections.content: After receiving the diwani of Bengal, the East India Company began systematic exploitation of Bengal's resources. The Company imposed heavy taxes on farmers and artisans, forcing many into poverty. The Permanent Settlement of 1793, introduced by Lord Cornwallis, made zamindars (landlords) the owners of land but required them to pay a fixed revenue to the Company. This system oppressed the actual cultivators and created a class of absentee landlords. The Company also destroyed Bengal's thriving textile industry by imposing high tariffs on Bengali goods while flooding the market with cheap British manufactured goods. The wealth drained from Bengal during this period contributed significantly to Britain's Industrial Revolution, while Bengal experienced deindustrialization and economic decline.

sections.title: The Bengal Famine of 1770 and Other Famines
sections.content: The Bengal Famine of 1770, also known as the Great Famine, was one of the deadliest famines in Indian history, resulting in the deaths of an estimated 10 million people, about one-third of Bengal's population. The famine was caused not by actual food scarcity but by the Company's exploitative revenue policies, hoarding by officials, and the export of grain for profit while people starved. During this famine, the Company continued to collect taxes mercilessly and even increased the tax rate. Subsequent famines occurred in 1783, 1866, and the Great Bengal Famine of 1943, which killed approximately 3 million people during World War II. These famines highlighted the devastating impact of colonial rule and the complete disregard of British authorities for the welfare of the Indian people.

sections.title: The Rise of Bengali Nationalism
sections.content: The British colonial exploitation sparked resistance and the growth of Bengali nationalism. Early resistance movements included the Sanyasi Rebellion (1763-1800), the Faraizi Movement led by Haji Shariatullah, and the Indigo Revolt (1859-60) where farmers protested against forced indigo cultivation. The formation of the Indian National Congress in 1885 and the Muslim League in 1906 provided political platforms for demanding rights. The partition of Bengal in 1905 by Lord Curzon sparked massive opposition and the Swadeshi Movement, which promoted Bengali goods and boycotted British products. The movement was eventually successful in forcing the annulment of the partition in 1911. These movements laid the foundation for the broader Indian independence movement and eventually led to the creation of Pakistan in 1947, of which Bengal became a part as East Pakistan.
